rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 21° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.71 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail. Use a longer rail or a higher-thrust motor.
Below the usual 5:1 minimum. Choose a higher-thrust motor or lighten the rocket.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Slow off the rail: 45 ft/s with an average thrust-to-weight of 3.7:1. Use a longer rail or a higher-thrust motor.
Strong weathercocking: the crosswind meets the rocket at up to 21° just after it leaves the rail, and it is 34° from vertical at burnout. Use a longer rail or a faster motor, or wait for less wind.

Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 35° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Chute opens 1.3 s after apogee at 46 ft/s
Average thrust-to-weight is 3.7:1, below the usual 5:1 minimum

Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.86 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 4.0 s after apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 10° from vertical)
Chute opens 4.0 s after apogee, at 101 ft/s and 219 ft below apogee. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.0 s the airspeed is 130% of the estimated flutter speed (337 ft/s at 290 ft), for fins of Balsa (shear modulus about 0.1 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.

example-1|calm.label: example-1|calm
rso: Below 1 caliber. Add 2.32 oz of nose weight at mid-nose or larger fins before flying.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 0° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.91 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 1.56 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight comes close to Mach 1, where stability estimates are less certain. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 5.2 s after apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 212% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Unstable or near-unstable (0.85 cal). Add nose weight.
Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 1° from vertical)
Chute opens 5.2 s after apogee, at 49 ft/s and 205 ft below apogee. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.8 s the airspeed is 212% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s at 1,100 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (25 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: Below 1 caliber. Add 2.32 oz of nose weight at mid-nose or larger fins before flying.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 13° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.54 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 7.73 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight comes close to Mach 1, where stability estimates are less certain. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 5.5 s after apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 212% of the estimated flutter speed (500 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Unstable or near-unstable (0.85 cal). Add nose weight.
Noticeable weathercocking: up to 13° angle of attack off the rail, and it is 18° from vertical at burnout.
Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 18° from vertical)
Chute opens 5.5 s after apogee, at 149 ft/s and 432 ft below apogee. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.8 s the airspeed is 212% of the estimated flutter speed (500 ft/s at 1,055 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (25 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.07 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.89 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 1.96 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight comes close to Mach 1, where stability estimates are less certain. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 4.5 s after apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 214% of the estimated flutter speed (504 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 9° from vertical)
Chute opens 4.5 s after apogee, at 132 ft/s and 309 ft below apogee. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.89 cal at 7° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+2.1 s the airspeed is 214% of the estimated flutter speed (504 ft/s at 1,519 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (26 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.07 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.89 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 1.96 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight comes close to Mach 1, where stability estimates are less certain. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
The chute is set to open at the motor ejection charge, but the motor is plugged: nothing opens and the rocket comes down ballistic.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 214% of the estimated flutter speed (504 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 9° from vertical)
The chute is set to open at the motor ejection charge, but the motor is plugged (Motor tab, Motor Delay): nothing opens and the rocket comes down ballistic.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.89 cal at 7° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+2.1 s the airspeed is 214% of the estimated flutter speed (504 ft/s at 1,519 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (26 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.07 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.89 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 1.96 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight comes close to Mach 1, where stability estimates are less certain. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 5.5 s before apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 214% of the estimated flutter speed (504 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 9° from vertical)
Chute opens 5.5 s before apogee, at 221 ft/s. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.89 cal at 7° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+2.1 s the airspeed is 214% of the estimated flutter speed (504 ft/s at 1,519 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (26 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.

Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.

example-2|wind.label: example-2|wind
rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length

1.52 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.46 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 16° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.45 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 7.61 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Noticeable weathercocking: up to 16° angle of attack off the rail, and it is 19° from vertical at burnout.

Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 21° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.45 cal at 16° to the airflow in this wind.
The H148 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.4 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.21 cal is only 8% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 4.42 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.84 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 2.88 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.84 cal at 6° to the airflow in this wind.
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.4 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.21 cal is only 8% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 4.42 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.84 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 2.88 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 12.2 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 12.2 s before apogee (737 ft, 620 ft/s) while the parachute is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

rso: Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.4 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.21 cal is only 8% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 4.42 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.

In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.84 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 2.88 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 2.7 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.7 s before apogee (3,546 ft, 98 ft/s) while the parachute is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.7 s before apogee (3,546 ft, 98 ft/s) while the parachute is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.84 cal at 6° to the airflow in this wind.
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 19° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.51 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Noticeable weathercocking: up to 18° angle of attack off the rail, and it is 25° from vertical at burnout.

Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 25° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Main descent is fast (24 ft/s). Consider a larger main.
The H148 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.80 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 8.2 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 8.2 s before apogee (2,458 ft, 315 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 9° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 8.2 s before apogee (2,458 ft, 315 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Main descent is fast (24 ft/s). Consider a larger main.
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.80 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 2.7 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.7 s before apogee (3,498 ft, 101 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 9° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.7 s before apogee (3,498 ft, 101 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Main descent is fast (24 ft/s). Consider a larger main.
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length

1.54 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.52 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.22 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length

1.54 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.52 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.22 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 14.3 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 14.3 s before apogee (802 ft, 689 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 14.3 s before apogee (802 ft, 689 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length

1.54 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.52 oz of nose weight at mid-nose.
In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.22 cal.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 4.8 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 4.8 s before apogee (4,356 ft, 168 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 4.8 s before apogee (4,356 ft, 168 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
The J381 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
